Use caution when handling the leaves,' and UF/IFAS EDIS ST441 independently confirms 'basal leaflets that are modified into sharp 2–3-inch-long spines' -- a puncture-injury hazard from handling the foliage, distinct from any toxicity concern (this species is tagged non-toxic to pets).

chill_damage_f: left null. UF/IFAS EDIS ST441 gives 'cold hardy to USDA zone 10A (30°F), but... widely grown in zone 9B (25°F)' -- a landscape hardiness-zone floor reflecting survival/growability, not a stated damage-onset temperature. Clemson's Indoor Palms factsheet separately states 'Most houseplant palms need temperatures above 45°F to prevent chilling damage,' but that is general 'most houseplant palms' wording from the page's shared introductory section, not a Phoenix-roebelenii-specific figure -- this catalog excluded the identical general line for another species (Parlor Palm) profiled on the same page, so it was treated the same way here. RHS separately rates the species Hardiness H1B ('can be grown outside in the summer, 10-15°C'), a UK seasonal-placement/growing-condition band, not a stated frost/chill damage-onset temperature, consistent with how this catalog treats RHS hardiness ratings elsewhere.

humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: left null. NC State's only humidity statement is 'It also prefers medium to high humidity' -- a two-tier range rather than a single low/average/high category, so no enum value was forced. Clemson's Indoor Palms factsheet separately notes that indoor air 'below 50%' merits supplemental humidity measures (gravel tray, humidifier, misting), but that is general, multi-species 'Indoor Palms' remediation guidance rather than a stated ideal-humidity percentage for this species specifically.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source gives a foot-candle light value for this species; only qualitative descriptions ('medium to high light,' 'bright indirect sunlight,' 'bright indirect light with shade from hot sun') were found.

direct_sun_hours_max: left null. NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours...)' and 'Partial Shade (...2-6 hours)' parentheticals are the site's fixed, generic definitional text for those light-category labels (the same wording is used site-wide for any species carrying those tags), not a measured or recommended sun-hours figure specific to this species.

soil_drainage: left null. NC State's own Soil Drainage tag for this species is the bare category 'Good Drainage' with no accompanying 'Occasionally Dry'/'Occasionally Wet' qualifier, and RHS gives only the bare 'Moist but well-drained' phrase -- both genuinely ambiguous per the fast/moderate/moisture_retentive definitions. NC State's own prose pulls in two directions: 'Keep the growing medium slightly moist during the growing season' argues against a dry-tolerant 'fast' reading, while 'do not overwater as doing so can cause root rot' argues against a 'moisture_retentive' reading, so no single enum value was assigned.

records.toxicity_detail: UF/IFAS's South Florida ornamental-palm guide flags this species with "Irritating Fruits? Yes," explained elsewhere on the same page as fruit containing skin-irritating chemicals that should not be handled without gloves. That caution names no animal (it is framed as a human/child handling hazard), so it does not by itself establish toxicity to cats or dogs.
unknowns: No admissible source (NC State, Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS EDIS/Ask IFAS, RHS, Penn State, Maryland, or UGA CAES) has a page discussing whether Cat Palm is toxic/non-toxic to cats or dogs specifically. Clemson's dedicated 'Pet-Safe Indoor Houseplants: What's Safe for Cats and Dogs' page names 'Parlor Palms (Chamaedorea elegans)' explicitly among its 10 non-toxic houseplants but does not mention Cat Palm/Chamaedorea cataractarum at all -- confirming the two species are treated separately and that Cat Palm's pet-safety status is not established by that source. toxic_to_pets is left null rather than inferred from the related species or from UF/IFAS's animal-unscoped 'irritating fruits' flag.

NC State Extension Plant Toolbox (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) has no dedicated page for Chamaedorea cataractarum -- checked directly (404) and via its Chamaedorea common-name grouping page, which lists only Chamaedorea elegans. This confirms no NC State content should be attributed to Cat Palm.

chill_damage_f and USDA hardiness zone: no admissible source gives a Cat-Palm-specific number. Clemson's Indoor Palms factsheet states a document-wide 'Most houseplant palms need temperatures above 45 °F to prevent chilling damage,' but that is general guidance covering every palm profiled in the factsheet (including the separately-treated Chamaedorea elegans), not a measurement specific to this species, so it was not used.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min come from Clemson's document-wide 'Most palms prefer...' statement, general guidance for the whole Indoor Palms factsheet rather than a Cat-Palm-specific measurement; night_f_max is not stated anywhere.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source states a species-specific humidity preference for Cat Palm (Clemson's Cat-Palm paragraph itself is silent on humidity; its general Problems section only gives a generic <50% RH troubleshooting threshold for houseplant palms broadly, not a stated preference for this species).

light_fc_min/light_fc_good: Clemson's foot-candle light-requirement table (a separate factsheet, 'Indoor Plants - Cleaning, Fertilizing, Containers & Light Requirements') lists Chamaedorea elegans (Low, 100 ft-c) and Chamaedorea erumpens (Medium) by name but does NOT include Chamaedorea cataractarum. Cat Palm's own blurb only says qualitatively that it 'will thrive in bright light,' with no ft-c figure, so these fields are left null rather than borrowed from a sibling species' table entry.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, direct_sun_hours_max, cool_rest_note: no admissible source gives any figure or description for these for this species.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: Clemson's general Culture section says only 'Fertilize only two to three times a year while the plant is actively growing during the spring and summer months' -- a word-based cadence and season name, not a literal day-interval or named months/strength, so per the no-derivation rule these are left null rather than computed.

soil_base/soil_drainage rely on Clemson's general palm potting-mix sentence ('porous...adequate moisture and excellent drainage'), which is document-wide guidance for the profiled indoor palms rather than a soil test specific to Cat Palm.

RHS's page for this species is a botanical-classification stub (family, synonyms, native range, name status) with no cultivation, hardiness, soil, or toxicity section, unlike more heavily documented RHS entries.

soil_base — removed on audit: Shares the soil_drainage citation and the same document-wide-not-species-specific problem: the record's own unknowns text calls this 'document-wide guidance for the profiled indoor palms rather than a soil test specific to Cat Palm,' the same standard used to null chill_damage_f/humidity/fertilize fields elsewhere in this record. 'standard_potting' is a plausible single-token value structurally, but its selection over leaving the field null is inconsistent with how the record treats equally-generic Clemson statements elsewhere.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The cited quote — 'Soil mixes for palms must be porous with plenty of organic matter to ensure both adequate moisture and excellent drainage' — explicitly says EXCELLENT drainage, yet the field value chosen is 'moderate.' That is a direct value/quote mismatch: the source used to justify this field does not support 'moderate' as the drainage characterization; if anything it supports a well-draining/excellent-drainage token. Additionally, like day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min, this is sourced from a passage the record itself elsewhere treats as too generic/document-wide to use (it nulls chill_damage_f, humidity, and fertilize fields from the same kind of 'most palms'/document-wide Clemson sentences), so its status as Cat-Palm-specific evidence is doubtful on top of the wording mismatch.

unknowns: The two admissible dedicated species pages disagree on the currently accepted scientific name: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists 'Peperomia argyraea' as current (with 'Peperomia argyreia' as a former name), while RHS's plant profile marks 'Peperomia argyreia' as the correct current name (synonym: Peperomia sandersii). scientific_name_accepted is left null because of this genuine conflict; see name_note.

'Watermelon Peperomia' -- the working name for this research task -- is also a well-attested name for this species: it is one of NC State's three listed common names, it is the heading Clemson HGIC uses for its own subsection on the species within a multi-species Peperomia spp. factsheet, and it is the name RHS's own genus-wide growing guide uses when introducing this species as 'probably the best-known species' of the genus. However, the two admissible pages dedicated solely to this one species (NC State and RHS) both lead with 'Watermelon Begonia' as their primary/title common name (RHS's page title is literally 'Peperomia argyreia | watermelon begonia', with 'watermelon peperomia' not even appearing in its own Other-common-names field), so 'Watermelon Begonia' was used for common_name per the dedicated-page sourcing tie-break rule.

day_f_min/day_f_max, humidity_need, soil_base, and all three fertilizing fields (fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength) rely on RHS's genus-level 'How to grow peperomia' guide rather than a page dedicated to this species alone. NC State's own structured tags are 'Good Drainage' + 'Moist' (which would mechanically map to moisture_retentive), yet NC State's own prose warns 'Avoid overwatering, as it can cause the corms to rot,' and Missouri Botanical Garden's Problems section separately states 'Overwatering can cause the corms to rot.' RHS meanwhile says the plant needs 'free-draining potting compost with added grit' and 'will not grow in wet compost,' yet its growing guide also instructs 'Don't let the plants dry out.' Because sources (and even single sources) want both moisture retention and sharp drainage at once, this was left null per the rule against picking a side in a genuine cross-source/same-source disagreement.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis left null: no admissible source gives a specific watering-frequency interval (e.g. 'every X days') or a moisture-check depth for Freesia; all guidance found is qualitative only ('water as needed,' 'don't let dry out,' 'avoid overwatering').

fertilize_active_months left null: no admissible source ties fertilizing to specific calendar months. Timing is described relative to growth stage instead ('after they are about 6 inches tall' per NC State; 'once the first buds are seen' per RHS), and planting schedules vary widely by climate/method (RHS: pots planted Aug-Dec for winter/spring bloom vs. outdoor UK planting in April; NC State: late-summer planting for winter bloom), so no universal month list could be given.

fertilize_strength left null: no admissible source states a dilution fraction (full/half/quarter strength) for fertilizing Freesia -- both NC State and RHS name a fertilizer type/interval but not a strength.

Corm-storage temperature conflict (not a schema field, noted for context): Missouri Botanical Garden instructs storing dormant corms in 'a cool dry location,' while NC State's structured Bulb Storage guidance and RHS's growing guide instead call for warm storage (NC State: 77-86 degrees F / 25-30 degrees C; RHS: about 26 degrees C / 80 degrees F at 75-80% humidity to 'ripen' the corms). cool_rest_note above reflects only the shared reduce-water/dig-up/store-dry pattern common to all sources, not a specific storage temperature, given this conflict.

Day/night temperature note (context for day_f/night_f values used): RHS's growing guide gives a notably different ambient temperature protocol for its UK pot-forcing method -- an initial cold-frame period at 5C (41F), then a winter greenhouse target of 10-15C (50-60F), with heat damage above 15C (which the RHS page itself parenthetically renders as '50F,' an apparent internal unit-conversion inconsistency on their part since 15C is closer to 59F). This is a distinct growing protocol from the 60-70F day / 40-55F night 'best' range that NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden both state directly and which was used for day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max here.

soil_base — removed on audit: Both citations backing soil_base ('standard_potting') actually describe a mix amended specifically for drainage, not a plain potting mix: NC State says 'organic-rich potting mix with coarse sand or crushed rocks to provide good drainage' (verified verbatim) and RHS says 'two-thirds peat-free John Innes No.2 potting compost and one-third horticultural grit' (verified verbatim) -- roughly a third of the RHS mix by volume is grit, not potting compost. Given that both admissible sources separately warn overwatering rots the corms, mapping this to generic 'standard_potting' risks under-communicating the load-bearing 'add grit/coarse sand' instruction that is common to both sources (unlike the moisture-vs-drainage tension that correctly drove soil_drainage to null, this one isn't a same-source contradiction -- both sources agree the base mix needs a drainage amendment). This is a plausible mis-mapping worth a second look, not a certain error, since the field's full enum vocabulary (e.g. whether a 'gritty_mix' or similar option exists) isn't visible from the record.

common_name — FLAGGED on audit (left as-is, needs manual review before landing): Live-checked ces.ncsu.edu/plants/freesia/, the only true 'dedicated page' cited here (a page for the genus Freesia). Its actual 'Common Name(s):' field reads 'Baboon Flower Freesias' -- i.e. it leads with 'Baboon Flower', then 'Freesias' (plural). It never lists bare 'Freesia' as a common name; NC State's own page separately tags 'Freesia' under Attributes as the Genus (scientific), not a common name. The record's own cited NC State quote proves this ('Common Name(s): Baboon Flower Freesias') yet the field value chosen is neither of those two names -- it is 'Freesia', which actually comes from the UGA source, a row in a multi-species 'Additional Bulbs to Try' table (fieldreport.caes.uga.edu/publications/B918), not a dedicated per-species page. So the citation that looks structurally on-point (NC State) does not actually support the chosen value, and the citation that does support the value (UGA) is a bundled table entry, not a dedicated page -- exactly the pattern this check is meant to catch. Per NC State's dedicated page, the correct leading common name would be 'Baboon Flower' (primary) or 'Freesias' (secondary). Note for context, not as an excuse for the bad citations: Missouri Botanical Garden's page (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid=264594; not cited for this field) has its own genuine 'Common Name:' field reading 'freesia', and that page is specifically about 'the large-flowered hybrids sold by florists' -- so 'Freesia' as a value is independently defensible, it is just not supported by the citations actually attached to it.

cool_rest_note — removed on audit: The underlying facts are correct (verified live), but citation #7's quote is not verbatim and does not appear anywhere on the page as written. I fetched https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/epiphyllum/growing-guide and full-text-searched it: there is no 'Winter resting period:' heading or sentence anywhere on the page (regex search for 'resting period' returned null). What the page actually says, in three separate places, is 'In winter, move to a cooler place, at 11-14C (52-57F), to encourage flowering' / 'In winter, move plants to a cooler location, about 11-14C (52-57F)' / 'Keep plants at 11-14C (52-57F) over winter, to stimulate flowering.' The cited string synthesizes a label ('Winter resting period:') that isn't on the page and presents it in quotation marks as if directly lifted. This is exactly the invented-quote failure mode the audit is watching for -- distinct from a wrong value, since the temperature figures and the 'to encourage flowering' purpose are independently confirmed true elsewhere on the same page. Citation #6 (the 6-week post-flowering rest quote from the RHS species page) IS verbatim -- confirmed via direct page-text extraction: '...keep just moist for 6 weeks after flowering to allow a rest period.'

fertilize_active_months — removed on audit: The cited quote -- 'To encourage flowering use an application of low nitrogen fertilizer once at the end of February and again in early November. Do not fertilize plants during December or January.' -- is verbatim and real (confirmed in Clemson's Orchid Cactus subsection), but it does not, by itself, 'name the specific months in which orchid cacti are fed' as the claim asserts. It names exactly two isolated flowering-boost applications (end of Feb, early Nov) plus an exclusion (Dec/Jan); it says nothing about March-October. The sentence that actually justifies a continuous Feb-Nov feeding window -- 'Plants should receive balanced fertilizer once a month from spring to fall' -- appears in the same Clemson paragraph but was never quoted or cited. Read together, the full paragraph does plausibly support [2..11], so the VALUE is likely fine, but the citation as constructed doesn't establish it and should be corrected to include the 'once a month from spring to fall' sentence. Separately, RHS's own species-detail page (rhs.org.uk/plants/32100/...) states a third, much sparser cadence -- 'apply a high potash fertiliser 3 or 4 times' during growth -- which is silent on which months but was not surfaced anywhere in the unknowns as a third conflicting data point.

name_note — removed on audit: Sub-claim 1 (the 8-name list: Dutchman's Pipe Cactus, Jungle Cactus, Lady of the Night, Night-blooming Cactus, Night-blooming Cereus, Night Queen, Orchid Cactus, Queen of the Night) is accurate -- verified verbatim against NC State's 'Common Name(s)' list. Sub-claim 2 is the problem: citation #4's claim label asserts the epithet is 'a Greek compound describing the petal shape,' but the quoted NC State text it cites says the opposite of 'shape' -- it says oxy- means 'sour' and states 'It presumably accurately describes their taste, although this plant is not known to have edible flowers' (verified live, exact match). The source is explicitly discussing a taste attribute, not petal shape. This is a claim-label/quote mismatch, not a fabricated quote -- the quote itself is verbatim and real, but it does not say what the claim asserts it says. (The final name_note field text sidesteps this by staying vague -- 'describing its petals' -- so the field text itself isn't wrong, but the supporting citation is, and should be corrected to stop calling this a shape descriptor.)

fertilize cadence conflict: RHS's species page gives a much sparser 'apply a high potash fertiliser 3 or 4 times' during growth (no months named); Clemson's monthly spring-to-fall schedule is the one encoded in fertilize_active_months.

unknowns: This record is exclusively about the epiphytic true cactus Rhipsalis baccifera (family Cactaceae), commonly called "mistletoe cactus" because its small round white/pink berries resemble mistletoe berries -- it is NOT the parasitic, hemiparasitic mistletoe (Phoradendron leucarpum, order Santalales) already catalogued separately in this collection as "American Mistletoe." No fact, quote, or citation in this record was drawn from any source describing that unrelated parasitic plant; every citation here is specific to Rhipsalis baccifera pages on plants.ces.ncsu.edu and rhs.org.uk.

Of the ten admissible domains, only plants.ces.ncsu.edu and www.rhs.org.uk returned a dedicated, species-specific page for this plant. Targeted searches on hgic.clemson.edu, plantfinder.mobot.org/missouribotanicalgarden.org, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, and fieldreport.caes.uga.edu found no page naming Rhipsalis baccifera or 'mistletoe cactus.'

night_f_min, night_f_max: NC State gives only one unified statement -- 'The plant also prefers temperatures between 60 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit' -- with no day/night split, so per this catalog's convention for such single-range statements the figures were applied only to day_f_min/day_f_max, and the night fields were left null rather than assumed identical.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source states an explicit cold-damage-onset or frost threshold for this species. RHS rates it Hardiness H1B ('can be grown outside in the summer (10 - 15)'), but consistent with how this catalog treats RHS hardiness ratings elsewhere, that is a UK seasonal-outdoor-placement band describing a minimum growing-condition temperature, not a stated damage-onset figure, so it was not used.
humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source gives a numeric relative-humidity percentage for this species; both NC State and RHS use only the qualitative phrase 'high humidity.'
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives foot-candle light values for this species.

soil_drainage: NC State's own structured Soil Drainage tags for this species are 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist' only (no 'Occasionally Dry' or 'Occasionally Wet' counterpart), which would mechanically map to moisture_retentive per this catalog's tag rule. But the same NC State page separately warns 'Overwatering can cause mushy stems and root rot' and asks for a 'well-drained, gritty, cactus potting mix' watered only 'when the soil feels dry' -- qualitative evidence pointing away from a wet-tolerant classification. RHS's own Moisture field is a bare 'Well-drained' with no distinguishing detail. Given this same-source tension and the underspecified RHS tag, soil_drainage is left null rather than forcing a token in either direction.

soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: NC State's structured Soil pH tag for this species is 'Acid (<6.0)' alone, which in isolation would support soil_ph_max=6.0. But RHS's own pH field for this exact species reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' -- effectively no restriction -- directly contradicting NC State's narrower acid-only bound. Given this cross-source disagreement, no numeric soil_ph value was taken.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a soil-check depth or an explicit day-count watering interval for either the growing season or winter dormancy; both NC State and RHS describe watering only qualitatively ('when the soil feels dry,' 'water moderately when in growth,' 'keep just moist in winter').

fertilize_interval_days: RHS's only fertilizing instruction ('apply a dilute low nitrogen fertiliser monthly') uses the word 'monthly,' a named cadence rather than a literal day-count figure; per this catalog's standing rule against silently converting 'monthly' into 30, no value was recorded. No other admissible source gives fertilizer guidance for this species.
fertilize_active_months: RHS ties fertilizing only to 'when in growth' generally, without naming specific calendar months.

fertilize_strength: RHS's instruction to use a 'dilute low nitrogen fertiliser' describes the fertilizer's formulation and general dilution intent, not one of the fixed full/half/quarter strength fractions; no admissible source states a specific dilution ratio.

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_sun: RHS's Position field lists 'Full sun, Partial shade' for this species, but NC State's own species-specific structured Light field offers only the single option 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' -- no full-sun option at all -- and NC State's own prose separately warns 'Direct sunlight can cause scorching of the stems.' Given NC State's dedicated species page both omits a full-sun option and explicitly warns of scorch damage, full_sun was excluded and only part_shade (agreed on by both sources) was kept.
